claim: Avoidance is a prevalent feature of anxiety-related psychopathology.
source: Although avoidance is a prevalent feature of anxiety-related psychopathology, differences in the measurement of avoidance between humans and non-human animals hinder our progress in its theoretical understanding and treatment.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact in the abstract and introduction, drawing on general scientific knowledge about anxiety disorders.

claim: Differences in the measurement of avoidance between humans and non-human animals hinder progress in theoretical understanding and treatment.
source: Although avoidance is a prevalent feature of anxiety-related psychopathology, differences in the measurement of avoidance between humans and non-human animals hinder our progress in its theoretical understanding and treatment.
evidence: This is presented as a problem motivating the current study, based on inference from the state of the field.

claim: Participants who experienced greater task-induced anxiety avoided choices associated with punishment, even when this resulted in lower overall reward.
source: In a large online study (n = 372), participants who experienced greater task-induced anxiety avoided choices associated with punishment, even when this resulted in lower overall reward.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: The effect of anxiety on avoidance was explained by greater individual sensitivities to punishment relative to rewards.
source: Computational modelling revealed that this effect was explained by greater individual sensitivities to punishment relative to rewards.
evidence: This finding is derived from computational modeling of the experimental data.

claim: The findings were replicated in an independent sample of n = 627.
source: We replicated these findings in an independent sample (n = 627)
evidence: This is a direct statement about replication data collected in the study.

claim: Measures of task performance showed fair-to-excellent reliability when retested 1 week later.
source: we also found fair-to-excellent reliability of measures of task performance in a sub-sample retested 1 week later (n = 57).
evidence: This is based on test-retest reliability data from the study.

claim: Excessive avoidance is a hallmark symptom of pathological anxiety.
source: Such excessive avoidance is a hallmark symptom of pathological anxiety (Barlow, 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Barlow, 2002.

claim: Avoidance biases during approach-avoidance conflict are thought to drive the development and maintenance of anxiety-related disorders.
source: avoidance biases during approach-avoidance conflict are thought to drive the development and maintenance of anxiety-related (Hayes, 1976; Stein and Paulus, 2009; Aupperle and Paulus, 2010; Mkrtchian et al., 2017; Struijs et al., 2018) and other psychiatric disorders (Aldao et al., 2010; Kakoschke et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the Geller-Seifter conflict test, rodents decide whether or not to press a lever that is associated with the delivery of both food pellets and shocks.
source: For example, in the 'Geller-Seifter conflict test' (Geller et al., 1962), rodents decide whether or not to press a lever that is associated with the delivery of both food pellets and shocks, thus inducing a conflict.
evidence: This describes a specific experimental paradigm with a citation.

claim: Anxiolytic drugs typically increase lever presses during the Geller-Seifter conflict test.
source: Anxiolytic drugs typically increase lever presses during the test (Treit et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Treit et al., 2010.

claim: Translational approaches benefit the study of avoidance and its relevance to mental ill-health.
source: Translational approaches, specifically when equivalent tasks are used to measure the same cognitive construct in humans and non-human animals, benefit the study of avoidance and its relevance to mental ill-health for two important reasons (Bach, 2022; Pike et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bach, 2022 and Pike et al., 2021.

claim: Precise causal manipulations of neural circuitry such as chemo/optogenetics are only feasible in non-human animals.
source: First, precise causal manipulations of neural circuitry such as chemo/optogenetics are only feasible in non-human animals, whereas only humans can verbalise their subjective experiences
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about current scientific capabilities.

claim: Only humans can verbalise their subjective experiences.
source: First, precise causal manipulations of neural circuitry such as chemo/optogenetics are only feasible in non-human animals, whereas only humans can verbalise their subjective experiences
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about human and non-human animal capabilities.

claim: Computational validity has been proposed as the primary basis for evaluating the validity of translational measures.
source: This criterion, which has been termed computational validity, has been proposed as the primary basis for evaluating the validity of translational measures (Redish et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Redish et al., 2022.

claim: Rodents typically avoid anxiogenic regions in exploration-based paradigms.
source: Rodents typically avoid such regions, which can take the form of tall, exposed platforms as in the elevated plus maze (Pellow et al., 1985), or large open spaces as in the open-field test (Hall, 1934).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pellow et al., 1985 and Hall, 1934.

claim: Similar avoidance behaviors have been observed in humans when virtual reality was used to translate the elevated plus maze.
source: Similar behaviours have been observed in humans when virtual reality was used to translate the elevated plus maze (Biedermann et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Biedermann et al., 2017.

claim: Individual differences in self-reported anxiety are associated with greater avoidance of exposed/open regions of space in translational tasks.
source: their predictive validity is supported by findings that individual differences in self-reported anxiety are associated with greater avoidance of the exposed/open regions of space (Walz et al., 2016; Biedermann et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Walz et al., 2016 and Biedermann et al., 2017.

claim: The computations underlying free movement are difficult to model as the action space is large and complex.
source: The computations underlying free movement are difficult to model as the action space is large and complex (consisting of two-dimensional directions, velocity, etc.), which makes it difficult to understand the precise cognitive mechanisms underlying avoidance in these tasks.
evidence: This is an inference based on the complexity of modeling spatial behavior.

claim: Evidence from economic decision-making suggests that explicit offers of probabilistic outcomes can impact decision-making differently compared to when probabilistic contingencies need to be learned from experience.
source: Moreover, evidence from economic decision-making suggests that explicit offers of probabilistic outcomes can impact decision-making differently compared to when probabilistic contingencies need to be learned from experience (referred to as the 'description-experience gap'; Hertwig and Erev, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hertwig and Erev, 2009.

claim: Participants chose the option with relatively higher reward probability across trials.
source: As expected, across trials participants chose (i.e. approached) the option with relatively higher reward probability (β = 0.98 ± 0.03, p < 0.001; Figure 2a and c).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Participants avoided the conflict option when it was more likely to produce the punishment.
source: At the same time, they avoided the conflict option when it was more likely to produce the punishment (β = –0.33 ± 0.04, p < 0.001; Figure 2a and d).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Task-induced anxiety significantly interacted with punishment probability in predicting choice.
source: Here, task-induced anxiety significantly interacted with punishment probability (β = –0.10 ± 0.04, p = 0.022; Figure 2a)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2.

claim: More anxious individuals were proportionately less willing to choose the conflict option during times it was likely to produce the punishment, relative to less-anxious individuals.
source: such that more anxious individuals were proportionately less willing to choose the conflict option during times it was likely to produce the punishment, relative to less-anxious individuals (Figure 2e).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data and shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The winning computational model included reward- and punishment-specific learning rates, and reward- and punishment-specific sensitivities.
source: The winning model in both the discovery and replication samples included reward- and punishment-specific learning rates, and reward- and punishment-specific sensitivities (i.e. four parameters in total; Figure 3a and b).
evidence: This is based on model comparison analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Parameter recovery from the winning model was excellent, with Pearson's r values between data-generating and recovered parameters ranging from 0.77 to 0.86.
source: Parameter recovery from the winning model was excellent, with Pearson's r values between data-generating and recovered parameters ranging from 0.77 to 0.86 (Appendix 4—figure 1).
evidence: This is based on parameter recovery analysis reported in the appendix.

claim: The punishment learning rate was significantly and negatively correlated with task-induced anxiety in the discovery sample.
source: The punishment learning rate and reward-punishment sensitivity index were significantly and negatively correlated with task-induced anxiety in the discovery sample (punishment learning rate: Kendall's τ = –0.088, p = 0.015
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: The reward-punishment sensitivity index was significantly and negatively correlated with task-induced anxiety in the discovery sample.
source: The punishment learning rate and reward-punishment sensitivity index were significantly and negatively correlated with task-induced anxiety in the discovery sample (punishment learning rate: Kendall's τ = –0.088, p = 0.015; reward-punishment sensitivity index: τ = –0.099, p = 0.005; Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mediating effect of the reward-punishment sensitivity index was over four times larger than the mediating effect of the punishment learning rate.
source: This suggested that the mediating effect of the reward-punishment sensitivity index (standardised β = –0.009 ± 0.003, p = 0.003) was over four times larger than the mediating effect of the punishment learning rate, which did not reach the threshold as a significant mediator (standardised β = –0.002 ± 0.001, p = 0.052; Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on mediation analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Anxiety, depression, and experiential avoidance symptoms were all significantly and positively correlated with task-induced anxiety.
source: Anxiety, depression, and experiential avoidance symptoms were all significantly and positively correlated with task-induced anxiety (p < 0.001; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of questionnaire and task data.

claim: Overall choice proportion showed good reliability in split-half analysis.
source: Overall choice proportion showed good reliability (discovery sample r = 0.63; replication sample r = 0.63; Appendix 5—figure 1).
evidence: This is based on split-half reliability analysis.

claim: The model parameters showed good-to-excellent reliability in split-half analysis.
source: The model parameters showed good-to-excellent reliability (model-derived r values ranging from 0.61 to 0.85 [0.76–0.92 after Spearman-Brown correction]; Appendix 5—figure 1).
evidence: This is based on split-half reliability analysis.

claim: Task-induced anxiety, overall proportion of conflict option choices, and the model parameters demonstrated fair to excellent test-retest reliability.
source: Task-induced anxiety, overall proportion of conflict option choices, and the model parameters demonstrated fair to excellent reliability (reliability indices ranging from 0.4 to 0.77; Appendix 6—figure 1), except for the punishment learning rate which showed a model-derived reliability of r = –0.45.
evidence: This is based on test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: The punishment learning rate showed poor test-retest reliability with a model-derived reliability of r = –0.45.
source: Task-induced anxiety, overall proportion of conflict option choices, and the model parameters demonstrated fair to excellent reliability (reliability indices ranging from 0.4 to 0.77; Appendix 6—figure 1), except for the punishment learning rate which showed a model-derived reliability of r = –0.45.
evidence: This is based on test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: Task-induced anxiety was significantly lower in the second session compared to the first session.
source: Practice effects analyses showed that task-induced anxiety and the punishment learning rate were also significantly lower in the second session (anxiety: t56 = 2.21, p = 0.031
evidence: This is based on practice effects analysis comparing test and retest sessions.

claim: The punishment learning rate was significantly lower in the second session compared to the first session.
source: Practice effects analyses showed that task-induced anxiety and the punishment learning rate were also significantly lower in the second session (anxiety: t56 = 2.21, p = 0.031; punishment learning rate: t56 = 2.24, p = 0.029)
evidence: This is based on practice effects analysis comparing test and retest sessions.

claim: The task shows sufficient face validity when compared to the Vogel/Geller-Seifter conflict tests.
source: The task shows sufficient face validity when compared to the Vogel/Geller-Seifter conflict tests; the design involves a series of choices between an action associated with high reward and punishment, or low reward and no punishment, and these contingencies must be learned.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of task designs.

claim: Avoidance responses were positively associated with task-induced anxiety, lending support for the construct validity of the measure.
source: That avoidance responses were positively associated with task-induced anxiety also lends support for the construct validity of our measure, given the theoretical links between anxiety and avoidance under approach-avoidance conflict (Hayes, 1976; Stein and Paulus, 2009; Aupperle and Paulus, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings and theoretical considerations, supported by citations.

claim: The empirical effect size of the relationship between anxiety and avoidance was small (|r|~0.13).
source: However, we note that the empirical effect size was small (|r|~0.13)
evidence: This is based on the observed correlation coefficients in the data.

claim: Non-human animals rely on reinforcement learning strategies during reward and punishment learning.
source: There exist many studies showing that non-human animals rely on similar strategies during reward and punishment learning (Schultz, 2013; Mobbs et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Schultz, 2013 and Mobbs et al., 2020.

claim: The traditional view has long been that anxiety is associated with greater automatic sensitivity to punishments and threats.
source: The traditional view has long been that anxiety is associated with greater automatic sensitivity to punishments and threats (i.e. that anxious individuals show a negative bias in information processing; Bishop, 2007), due to amygdala hypersensitivity (Mathews and Mackintosh, 1998; Hartley and Phelps, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bishop, 2007; Mathews and Mackintosh, 1998; and Hartley and Phelps, 2012.

claim: Subsequent studies have found inconsistent findings relative to the hypothesis that anxiety is associated with greater automatic sensitivity to punishments and threats.
source: However, subsequent studies have found inconsistent findings relative to this hypothesis (Bishop and Gagne, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bishop and Gagne, 2018.

claim: The relative sensitivity to punishment over reward provided a better explanation of anxiety's effect on behaviour than a straightforward link between anxiety and punishment sensitivity.
source: We found that, rather than a straightforward link between anxiety and punishment sensitivity, the relative sensitivity to punishment over reward provided a better explanation of anxiety's effect on behaviour.
evidence: This is based on the mediation analysis results from the study.

claim: A recent computational meta-analysis of reinforcement learning studies showed that symptoms of anxiety and depression are associated with elevated punishment learning rates.
source: Notably, although a recent computational meta-analysis of reinforcement learning studies showed that symptoms of anxiety and depression are associated with elevated punishment learning rates (Pike and Robinson, 2022), we did not observe this pattern in our data.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pike and Robinson, 2022.

claim: The direction of the effect of anxiety on punishment learning rate can depend on the form of anxiety, where cognitive anxiety may be associated with elevated learning rates, but somatic anxiety may show the opposite pattern.
source: However, other work has suggested that the direction of this effect can depend on the form of anxiety, where cognitive anxiety may be associated with elevated learning rates, but somatic anxiety may show the opposite pattern (Wise and Dolan, 2020)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wise and Dolan, 2020.

claim: Parameter values are highly dependent on task design.
source: Additionally, parameter values are highly dependent on task design (Eckstein et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Eckstein et al., 2022.

claim: The discovery sample had a significantly greater proportion of female participants than the replication sample (59% vs 52%).
source: The discovery sample had a significantly greater proportion of female participants than the replication sample (59% vs 52%, χ2 = 4.64, p = 0.031).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of demographic data between samples.

claim: The average age was significantly different across discovery and replication samples.
source: The average age was also significantly different across samples (discovery sample mean = 37.7, SD = 10.3, replication sample mean = 34.3, SD = 10.4; t785.5 = 5.06, p < 0.001).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of demographic data between samples.

claim: Sex was significantly associated with choice in the hierarchical logistic regression in the discovery sample, with males being more likely to choose the conflict option.
source: While sex was significantly associated with choice in the hierarchical logistic regression in the discovery sample (β = 0.16 ± 0.07, p = 0.028) with males being more likely to choose the conflict option
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The sex effect on choice was not evident in the replication sample.
source: this pattern was not evident in the replication sample (β = 0.08 ± 0.06, p = 0.173)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Participants reported a moderate level of task-induced anxiety on average (mean rating of 21, SD = 14).
source: On average, participants reported a moderate level of task-induced anxiety (mean rating of 21, SD = 14; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is based on subjective ratings collected in the study and shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Task-induced anxiety was correlated with the proportion of conflict/safe option choices made by each participant, with greater anxiety corresponding to a preference for the safe option.
source: Task-induced anxiety was significantly associated with multiple aspects of task performance. At the most basic level, task-induced anxiety was correlated with the proportion of conflict/safe option choices made by each participant across all trials, with greater anxiety corresponding to a preference for the safe option over the conflict option (permutation-based non-parametric correlation test: Kendall's τ = –0.074, p = 0.033)
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Participants gave a mean unpleasantness rating of 31.7 (SD = 12.8) for the punishments.
source: When asked to rate the unpleasantness of the punishments from 'Not at all' to 'Extremely' (scored from 0 to 50, respectively), participants gave a mean rating of 31.7 (SD = 12.8).
evidence: This is based on subjective ratings collected in the study.

claim: The instances of clinically relevant anxiety symptoms were low in both the discovery (16%) and replication sample (20%).
source: Given that we recruited samples without any inclusion/exclusion criteria relating to mental health, the instances of clinically relevant anxiety symptoms, defined as a score of 10 or greater in the Generalised Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (Spitzer et al., 2006), were low in both the discovery (16%, 60 participants) and the replication sample (20%, 127 participants).
evidence: This is based on questionnaire data from the study.

claim: Only experiential avoidance symptoms were significantly correlated with the proportion of conflict/safe option choices in the discovery sample.
source: Only experiential avoidance symptoms were significantly correlated with the proportion of conflict/safe option choices (τ = –0.059, p = 0.010; Appendix 1—table 1)
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of questionnaire and task data.

claim: The correlation between experiential avoidance and proportion of conflict/safe option choices was not observed in the replication sample.
source: but this effect was not observed in the replication sample (τ = –0.029, p = 0.286).
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of questionnaire and task data.

claim: Experiential avoidance was significantly correlated with punishment learning rates in the discovery sample.
source: Experiential avoidance was also significantly correlated with punishment learning rates (Kendall's τ = –0.09, p = 0.024)
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of questionnaire and model parameter data.

claim: Experiential avoidance was significantly correlated with the reward-punishment sensitivity index in the discovery sample.
source: and the reward-punishment sensitivity index (τ = –0.09, p = 0.034) in the discovery sample.
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of questionnaire and model parameter data.

claim: The associations between experiential avoidance and punishment learning rates/reward-punishment sensitivity index were non-significant in the replication sample.
source: However, these associations were non-significant in the replication sample (p > 0.3)
evidence: This is based on correlation analysis of questionnaire and model parameter data.

claim: Comparing parameters across sexes revealed significant differences in reward sensitivity, which was lower in females.
source: Comparing parameters across sexes via Welch's t-tests revealed significant differences in reward sensitivity (t289 = –2.87, p = 0.004, d = 0.34; lower in females)
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model parameters between sexes.

claim: The reward-punishment sensitivity index was significantly lower in females compared to males in the discovery sample.
source: and consequently reward-punishment sensitivity index (t336 = –2.03, p = 0.043, d = 0.22; lower in females, i.e. more avoidance-driven).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model parameters between sexes.

claim: The sex difference in reward-punishment sensitivity index was replicated in the replication sample.
source: In the replication sample, we observed the same effect on reward-punishment sensitivity index (t626 = –2.79, p = 0.005, d = 0.22; lower in females).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model parameters between sexes.

claim: The sex difference in reward sensitivity did not replicate in the replication sample.
source: However, the sex difference in reward sensitivity did not replicate (p=0.441)
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model parameters between sexes.

claim: A significant sex difference in punishment sensitivity was observed in the replication sample.
source: although we did observe a significant sex difference in punishment sensitivity in the replication sample (t626 = 2.26, p = 0.024, d = 0.18).
evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of model parameters between sexes.

claim: The winning model was able to reproduce the proportion of conflict option choices over all trials in the observed data with high accuracy (r = 0.97).
source: These synthetic choice data closely resembled the actual choices made by the participants (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is based on posterior predictive checks shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The task was developed by adapting a paradigm from the non-human animal literature to study the same cognitive processes in human participants.
source: To address this, we developed a novel translational measure of anxiety-related avoidance in the form of an approach-avoidance reinforcement learning task, by adapting a paradigm from the non-human animal literature to study the same cognitive processes in human participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and methodology.

claim: The task is based on the 'restless bandit' design.
source: We developed a novel approach-avoidance conflict task, based on the 'restless bandit' design (Daw et al., 2006)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task design with a citation.

claim: The conflict option was generally more rewarding compared to the safe option across trials.
source: Unbeknownst to the participant, one of the options (which we refer to as the 'conflict' option – solid lines) was generally more rewarding compared to the other option (the 'safe' option – dashed line) across trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task design.

claim: The conflict option was the only option associated with a probability of producing an aversive sound.
source: However, the conflict option was also the only option of the two that was associated with a probability of producing an aversive sound (the probability that the safe option produced the aversive sound was 0 across all trials).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task design.

claim: The probabilities of observing each outcome given the choice of option fluctuated randomly and independently across trials.
source: The probabilities of observing each outcome given the choice of option fluctuated randomly and independently across trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task design.

claim: The correlations between the dynamic probabilities were negligible (mean Pearson's r = 0.06).
source: The correlations between these dynamic probabilities were negligible (mean Pearson's r = 0.06).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the task design parameters.

claim: On average, the conflict option was more likely to produce a reward than the safe option.
source: On average, the conflict option was more likely to produce a reward than the safe option.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1d and is a feature of the task design.

claim: Participants were not informed about the asymmetric feature of the task.
source: Participants were not informed about this asymmetric feature of the task, but they were told that the probabilities of observing the reward or the sound were independent and that they could change across trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The study was pre-registered at https://osf.io/8dm95.
source: after which the key effects-of-interest were retested in a pre-registered study (https://osf.io/8dm95) with an independent replication sample (n = 629).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methodology.

claim: The study had ethical approval from the University College London Research Ethics Committee (ID 15253/001).
source: The study had ethical approval from the University College London Research Ethics Committee (ID 15253/001).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants were recruited from Prolific.
source: We recruited participants from Prolific (https://www.prolific.com/).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the recruitment method.

claim: Participants were reimbursed at a rate of £7.50 per hour.
source: Participants were reimbursed at a rate of £7.50 per hour, and could earn a bonus of up to an additional £7.50 per hour based on their performance on the task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant compensation.

claim: Participants could earn a bonus of up to an additional £7.50 per hour based on their performance on the task.
source: Participants were reimbursed at a rate of £7.50 per hour, and could earn a bonus of up to an additional £7.50 per hour based on their performance on the task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant compensation.

claim: A total of 423 participants completed the initial study.
source: A total of 423 participants completed the initial study (mean age = 38, SD = 10, 59% female)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size.

claim: A total of 726 participants completed the replication study.
source: and 726 participants completed the replication study (mean age = 34, SD = 10, 51% female).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the sample size.

claim: 8% of participants in both discovery and replication samples were excluded for missing more than one auditory attention check.
source: Firstly, we excluded participants who missed a response to more than one auditory attention check (see above; 8% in both discovery and replication samples)
evidence: This is based on data quality exclusion criteria.

claim: 4% of the discovery sample and 6% of the replication sample were excluded for responding with the same response key on 20 or more consecutive trials.
source: Secondly, we excluded those who responded with the same response key on 20 or more consecutive trials (>10% of all trials; 4%/6% in discovery and replication samples, respectively)
evidence: This is based on data quality exclusion criteria.

claim: 1% of the discovery sample and 2% of the replication sample were excluded for not responding on 20 or more trials.
source: Lastly, we excluded those who did not respond on 20 or more trials (1%/2% in discovery and replication samples, respectively).
evidence: This is based on data quality exclusion criteria.

claim: Overall, 51 out of 423 (12%) participants were excluded in the discovery sample.
source: Overall, we excluded 51 out of 423 (12%) in the discovery sample
evidence: This is based on data quality exclusion criteria.

claim: Overall, 98 out of 725 (14%) participants were excluded in the replication sample.
source: and 98 out of 725 (14%) in the replication sample.
evidence: This is based on data quality exclusion criteria.

claim: The data exclusions had no effects on the main findings reported in the manuscript.
source: These exclusions had no effects on the main findings reported in the manuscript
evidence: This is based on sensitivity analyses comparing results with and without exclusions.

claim: Participants completed 200 trials which took 10 minutes on average across the sample.
source: Participants completed 200 trials which took 10 minutes on average across the sample.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the task duration.

claim: The aversive auditory stimuli consisted of combinations of female screams and high-frequency tones that were individually rated as highly aversive in a previous online study.
source: We used aversive auditory stimuli as our punishments in the reinforcement learning task, which consisted of combinations of female screams and high-frequency tones that were individually rated as highly aversive in a previous online study (Seow and Hauser, 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Seow and Hauser, 2022.

claim: All participants completed an open-source, validated auditory discrimination task to screen out those who were unlikely to be using headphones.
source: All participants completed an open-source, validated auditory discrimination task (Woods et al., 2017) to screen out those who were unlikely to be using headphones.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure with a citation.

claim: Participants could only continue to the main task if they achieved an accuracy threshold of five out of six trials in the headphone screening task.
source: Participants could only continue to the main task if they achieved an accuracy threshold of five out of six trials in this screening task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: The models assume that participants estimate the probabilities of observing a reward and punishment separately for each option.
source: Briefly, our models assume that participants estimate the probabilities of observing a reward and punishment separately for each punishment, and continually update these estimates after observing the outcomes of their actions.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the computational model assumptions.

claim: The models were fit using a hierarchical EM algorithm.
source: We fit the models using a hierarchical EM algorithm (Huys et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a direct statement about the modeling methodology with a citation.

claim: Models were compared using integrated Bayesian information criterion.
source: We compared evidence across models using integrated Bayesian information criterion (Huys et al., 2011) which integrates both model likelihood and model complexity into a single measure for model comparison.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model comparison methodology with a citation.

claim: Mediation was assessed using structural equation modelling with the 'lavaan' package in R.
source: Mediation was assessed using structural equation modelling with the 'lavaan' package in R (Rosseel, 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical methodology with a citation.

claim: Psychiatric symptoms were measured using the Generalised Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD7), Patient Health Questionnaire depression scale (PHQ8), and the Brief Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire (BEAQ).
source: Psychiatric symptoms were measured using the Generalised Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD7; Spitzer et al., 2006), Patient Health Questionnaire depression scale (PHQ8; Kroenke et al., 2009), and the Brief Experiential Avoidance Questionnaire (BEAQ; Gámez et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the measurement instruments with citations.

claim: The required sample size for test-retest reliability analysis was 50 participants.
source: The required sample size was thus 50 participants, based on a one-tailed significance threshold of 0.05 and 90% power.
evidence: This is based on a priori power analysis.

claim: ICC(3,1) coefficients were calculated to assess the reliability of model-agnostic measures.
source: We calculated ICCs coefficients to assess the reliability of our model-agnostic measures. Specifically, we used consistency-based ICC(3,1) (following the notation of Shrout and Fleiss, 1979).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical methodology with a citation.

claim: The data and code required to replicate the data analyses are available online at https://osf.io/m3zev/.
source: The data and code required to replicate the data analyses are available online at https://osf.io/m3zev/.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.
